prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: The chair asks us to fix the principle before the name, so I state mine. The prize should reward the discovery that opened the field, and here that is the physiology: Holst on proglucagon processing and the secretion and insulinotropic action of GLP-1, Drucker on GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and receptor action, and Mojsov on identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide. The therapy is the evidence that the discovery matters, and the citation says so by closing on incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity. The science is mature and independently replicated, with cardiovascular and renal outcome benefit from large randomised trials by several groups, so the only open question is credit. I keep a single B007 part. A second part cannot fit: B007 alone needs three names, and B004 would leave B007 with only Drucker and Holst, which would be a worse prize than one clean part.
statement.case_against: My configuration omits Knudsen, whose acylation-based half-life extension turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into once-daily and once-weekly drugs. A fair critic can say we honour the hormone and skip the step that produced the medicine. The Mojsov credit also rests on a priority claim I cannot verify from the supplied record, and Habener is not on the list. If the committee chose a development-centred citation, my configuration would be the weaker of the two. The record we have does not give me grounds to rank one claim as decisively stronger, so I hold the position on principle and not on proof.

responses.point: Sandberg argues that the long-acting analogue is the step without which there is no drug to credit, and that a Drucker, Holst and Knudsen citation naming both physiology and agonist development represents the chain honestly. He says he would accept the Mojsov trio if the committee wants a purely discovery-level prize.
responses.response: That concession is useful, because it makes the principle the whole disagreement. I accept that acylation was real science and decisive for the outcome trials, and I do not call it routine engineering. But the Nobel framing asks what was discovered, and the identity of the active peptide is a discovery that every later analogue depends on, whereas Knudsen's analogue depends on that discovery and on Holst's and Drucker's physiology. Your trio also names an industrial development, which exposes the prize to the charge of crowning a product, a charge that Mojsov's name does not raise. My answer to your worry about reading as a ruling on priority is the citation wording: it credits the identification of the active form and does not say who was first. I would move to your trio only if the committee states that this prize is for the development of the agonists, and I do not think it should.

responses.point: Svenningsson, the chair, prefers Knudsen as the third name because the medicine exists only through acylated analogues. He says Mojsov rests on a credit he cannot verify from the supplied text, and that he would move if the committee judges peptide identification more decisive.
responses.response: Your objection to Mojsov is unverifiability, and I share it, but it does not favour Knudsen. We cannot verify Mojsov's priority and we also cannot verify that omitting her is neutral, since leaving out the name credited in four openings is itself a decision about a disputed record. I take your point that this field has honoured the step that reaches patients, but the Medicine prizes closest to this one, where physiology and drugs are tightly linked, were anchored in the physiology and not in a specific product. On your question whether any trio can avoid reading as a ruling, the answer is no, and neither can yours. The better test is which citation is true as written. Mine is, because it claims the identification of the active form as a contribution, and the dispute over who identified it first is carried by the committee record and not by the text.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius would honour the discovery-level contributions and let the citation name the physiology, so the prize stays anchored in what was found and not in a product. She flags the risk of honouring a commercially mature class while the basic science goes to a contested trio.
responses.response: I agree with the anchoring and I take the risk you name seriously. The way to reduce it is to keep the citation strictly about the physiology and the active form, with the therapy as consequence and not as the object of the prize, as I have drafted it. I would add that the contested part is narrower than it looks: Holst and Drucker are fixed for all six of us, so the dispute concerns one name and one step. If the committee wants to avoid a ruling on priority, the least bad approach is to name the identification of the active form without any statement about who was first, and I would resist widening the citation to say anything about commercial development.

uncertainties: Whether the record supports Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide relative to Habener and others, which I have not verified and which remains the main risk to my configuration.
Whether the committee will settle the principle in favour of discovery or development, since that alone decides between Mojsov and Knudsen.
Whether a two-person June and Sadelain configuration for B041 is defensible given Eshhar and Gross, which matters only if B007 stalls.
Whether long-term safety and durability of incretin therapy in obesity should change the wording of the citation.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I co-authored the 2016 Science spatial-transcriptomics paper and have recorded co-authorship with Rickard Sandberg (eight works, not independently audited). No shortlisted candidate or credited name is connected to my documented research, publications or institutional record, and I report no need for recusal.
